# Development of bifunctional biosensors for sensing and dynamic control of glycolysis flux in metabolic engineering

![](images/73b60c3c1d8bf6da256b76273c8f513744fddf6d2fdf515e6046dc5510c280fa.jpg)

Yuan Zhu <sup>a</sup>, Ying Li <sup>a</sup>, Ya Xu <sup>a</sup>, Jian Zhang <sup>a</sup>, Linlin Ma <sup>a</sup>, Qingsheng Qi <sup>a,b,\*\*</sup>, Qian Wang <sup>a,\*</sup>

<sup>a</sup> National Glycoengineering Research Center, State Key Laboratory of Microbial Technology, Shandong University, Qingdao, 266237, PR China <sup>b</sup> CAS Key Lab of Biobased Materials, Qingdao Institute of Bioenergy and Bioprocess Technology, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Qingdao, 266101, PR China

## A R T I C L E I N F O

Keywords:   
Glycolysis flux   
Fructose-1,6-diphosphate   
Bifunctional biosensor   
Dynamic control   
Mevalonate

## A B S T R A C T

Glycolysis is the primary metabolic pathway in all living organisms. Maintaining the balance of glycolysis flux and biosynthetic pathways is the crucial matter involved in the microbial cell factory. Few regulation systems can address the issue of metabolic flux imbalance in glycolysis. Here, we designed and constructed a bifunctional glycolysis flux biosensor that can dynamically regulate glycolysis flux for overproduction of desired biochemicals. A series of positive-and negative-response biosensors were created and modified for varied thresholds and dynamic ranges. These engineered glycolysis flux biosensors were verified to be able to characterize in vivo fructose-1,6-diphosphate concentration. Subsequently, the biosensors were applied for fine-tuning glycolysis flux to effectively balance the biosynthesis of two chemicals: mevalonate and N-acetylglucosamine. A glycolysis fluxdynamically controlled Escherichia coli strain achieved a 111.3 g/L mevalonate titer in a 1L fermenter.

## 1. Introduction

Metabolic engineering refers to the targeted modification of cell metabolism and the redistribution of carbon, energy, and electrons to maximize cellular performance in terms of yield and productivity. Metabolic flux should be finely reprogrammed without disrupting cellular homeostasis (Keasling, 2012; Price et al., 2004; Schellenberger et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2002). To overcome the disadvantages of the static permanent knockout of a pathway, dynamic flux rewiring based on the sophisticated metabolite-responsive transcriptional-level regulation has been effectively introduced into the microbial cell factory for autonomous dynamic control of metabolic flux(Cress et al., 2015; Farmer and Liao, 2000; Holtz and Keasling, 2010; Ma et al., 2018). Furthermore, various genetically encoded biosensors that can respond to external environmental signals (O , temperature, and pH) and intracellular states (metabolites, growth period, stress response, and redox) have been reported(Brockman and Prather, 2015; Wu et al., 2018a; Xu et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2012). Of these biosensors, only a few have been created to respond to central metabolites such as pyruvate (Xu et al., 2020), D-erythrose 4-phosphate, and glycerate-3-phosphate (Ding et al., 2020) for fine-tuning the synthesis of glycolysis and central

metabolism related chemicals.

Glycolysis is the fundamental pathway of cell metabolism, and how the glycolysis rate and carbon yield can be increased are common concerns in the microbial cell factory. This is because high glycolysis flux can cause overflow metabolism and excess cell growth, whereas a low glycolysis rate can cause low cell growth and product titer. Therefore, the rational control of glycolysis flux using a timely autonomous glycolysis flux regulation method is extremely beneficial for optimizing cell factories and maintaining cellular homeostasis. Fructose-1,6- diphosphate(FBP), the key intermediate in glycolysis, plays a crucial role in flux sensing, namely acting as a “flux sensor.” Here, it regulates the lower glycolysis flux through the allosteric activation of pyruvate kinase (Pyk)(Waygood et al., 1976) to match the upper glycolysis flux, creating linear relationships between the glycolysis flux and FBP pool in Escherichia coli(Kochanowski et al., 2013) and in Saccharomyces cerevisiae(Christen and Sauer, 2011). Thus, glycolysis flux can be reflected by the concentration of intracellular FBP(Kochanowski et al., 2013). Cra (catabolite repressor/activator), a dual global regulator factor belonging to GalR-LacI superfamily(Chin et al., 1989; Leclerc et al., 1990), plays an important role in global metabolic regulation and controls dozens of genes in glycolysis and gluconeogenesis(Ishihama, 2010). FBP binds to concentration (Fig. 4A). The growth rate of these four strains increased with the increasing intracellular FBP concentration (Fig. 4B). To further verify the constructed glycolysis flux biosensors, a negative-response biosensor pL19 was used, of which the fluorescence output is negatively linearly related to the FBP concentration and glycolytic flux. The results showed that the fluorescence value of BW-pfkA, BW-ptsG, and BW-pykF at 18h were 11.32, 7.13, and 1.11 times higher than that of the control BW25113, respectively. The fluorescence value decreased with the increasing intracellular FBP concentration, following the order of BW $- p f k A > \mathrm { B W } - p t s G > \mathrm { B W } - p y k F > \mathrm { B W } 2 5 1 1 3 \mathrm { ( F i g . }$ 4C). The linear detection range of intracellular FBP with biosensor pL19 is about 0–50 mmol ${ \mathbf g } ^ { - 1 }$ dry cell weight (Supplementary Fig. 3C), and the intracellular FBP concentration of E. coli strain is generally 0–31 mM ${ \bf g } ^ { - 1 }$ dry cell weight (Fig. 4). Thus the detection range of our tuned biosensors can cover the in vivo concentration of FBP in the actual situation, indicating our tuning engineering is necessary and the tuned biosensors are suitable for practical use.

## 3.4. Dynamic control of glycolysis flux for high MVA production

MVA, a key precursor for the production of isoprenoids(Pitera et $\mathrm { a l . , }$ 2007), is a building block for sustainable polymer production(Xiong et al., 2014). We previously designed an EP-bifido pathway to improve the acetyl-CoA provision in MVA production by breaking down fructose-6-phosphate into acetyl phosphate through a phosphoketolase (Fxpk) involved in carbon rearrangement(Wang et al., 2019). In this EP-bifido pathway, natural glycolysis was blocked by permanent pfkA deletion to enhance the PP pathway flux for sufficient supply of fructose-6-phosphate and NADPH. With this EP-bifido pathway, engineered E. coli BWΔpfkA obtained an MVA production yield of 64.3 mol %. However, because of the severe suppression of growth and glucose uptake caused by pfkA knockout, the MVA production was only 11.02 $_ { g / \mathrm { L } }$ (Supplementary Fig. 6). In this study, to address the robustness problems in the natural glycolysis pathway, the glycolysis flux in the EP-bifido pathway was dynamically regulated by the developed glycolysis flux biosensors (Fig. 5A). First, the PP pathway flux was enhanced by replacing the promoter of zwf on the genome with a stronger promoter, namely $\mathrm { P _ { 2 3 1 0 9 , } }$ to obtain the strain BW- $\begin{array} { r } { \cdot \mathrm { P } _ { z w f } . : \mathrm { P } _ { 2 3 1 0 9 } . } \end{array}$ Then, we replaced the promoter $\mathrm { P } _ { p f k A }$ in $\mathbf { B } \mathbf { W }  – \mathbf { P } _ { z w f } . . \mathbf { P } _ { 2 3 1 0 9 }$ with two negative-response biosensor-controlled promoters, namely Ppam (pL19) and Ppar (pL25) (Fig. 5B), resulting in the strains BW-PMT and BW-PR. Because the EP-bifido pathway was dynamically controlled through sensing the in vivo FBP concentration, we called it the dynamic EP-bifido pathway, and we subsequently applied this pathway in MVA production. The experimental results revealed that with the dynamically regulated EP-bifido pathway, both engineered strains behaved with a strong glucose uptake capacity and fewer overflow metabolism compared with the control strain, BW-PMT accumulated less than 2.47 g/L acetate and BW-PR accumulated less than 0.1 g/L acetate and no other byproducts (Supplementary Fig. 6 and Supplementary Fig. 7). The highest MVA production was obtained by strain BW-PR, which produced 73.31 g/L MVA, and the carbon yield reached 63.00 mol% (Fig. 5D and Supplementary Fig. 6). This is the highest MVA production obtained in shake flask fermentation to date. It grew rapidly in the logarithmic phase and reached the stationary phase after 12 h (Fig. 5D), indicating that a downregulation of pfkA at this time switched the flux from glycolysis into the EP-bifido pathway and uncoupled growth and production. The dynamic regulation of the glycolysis biosensor was also confirmed by the in vivo mRNA level of pfkA as well as the FBP level (Fig. 5E, F and 5G). The decreased mRNA expression of $p f k A$ in the dynamic EP-bifido strain compared with the nonregulated strain indicated the effectiveness of pfkA inhibition (Fig. 5E and F). The intracellular FBP concentration of BW-PR was lower than the control strain $\mathbf { B } \mathbf { W }  – \mathbf { P } _ { z w f } . . \mathbf { P } _ { 2 3 1 0 9 }$ (Fig. 5G) and dropped suddenly after 15 h, indicating the glycolysis was timely and gradually blocked and more flux flowed into the EP-bifido pathway. This timely dynamic control showed a greater advantage than chemical inducers induction regulation. A previous work indicated the IPTG induced CRISPRi suppression on pfkA gene in the EP-bifido strain only yield 8.53 g/L MVA $\mathrm { ( L i ~ e t ~ a l . , ~ 2 0 2 1 ) }$ , 0.12 times of the MVA titer in BW-PR (73.31 g/L). This also indicated the importance of real-time sensing of FBP concentration for pfkA regulation. To further optimize the MVA production, strain BW-PR was then fermented in a 1-L fermenter (Fig. 5H). Finally, a 111.3 g/L MVA was produced after 120 h cultivation and no by-products were produced.

## 3.5. Dual regulation of glycolysis flux and GlcNAc biosynthesis

In GlcNAc biosynthesis, the substrate fructose-6-phosphate was the competitive precursor of glycolysis and GlcNAc synthesis, and the lower part of glycolysis was a competitive pathway for GlcNAc biosynthesis when glucose was used as the sole carbon source(Tamai et al., 2003; Wu et al., 2018b) (Fig. 6A). In this case, not only did $p f k A$ need to be downregulated but also glmS (encoding F6P aminotransferase) need to be upregulated for overproducing GlcNAc, because early-stage overexpression of glmS may cause bacterial lysis and the inhibition of cell growth(Deng et al., 2005) (Fig. 6A). To realize this, we replaced the promoter of pfkA in strain DN5 with two negative-response biosensor-controlled promoters, namely Ppam (pL19) and Ppar (pL25) (Fig. 6B), to obtain strains DN5-IM and DN5-PM, respectively. DN5, a modified DH5α strain, which knockout the gene nag, ackA, poxB, ldhA and nan, was constructed by our laboratory in previous studies. When they were engineered for GlcNAc production, strain DN5-IM finally produced 8.65 g/L GlcNAc, whereas the control strain DN5 only produced 0.46 g/L GlcNAc (Fig. 6F). The pfkA downregulated strains DN5-PM and DN5-IM exhibited lower growth and less glucose consumption compared with DN5 (Fig. 6C and Supplementary Fig. 8), indicating that flux regulating was effective for precisely downregulating the activity of glycolysis. For the dynamic activation of glmS, the glmS gene on pBac was changed to be controlled by the positive-response promoters P<sub>M23107</sub> (pL09) and P<sub>R23107-cra</sub> (pL18) to form pBacm and pBacar, respectively. And cra gene with its P<sub>23102</sub> promoter on pL18 were also cloned into pBacar (Fig. 6B). Strain DN5 was transformed with the plasmids pBacm and pBacar to obtain the strains DN5-GM and DN5-GAR. The dynamically regulated strains DN5-GM and DN5-GAR produced 6.33 and 7.98 g/L GlcNAc, respectively, which were much higher compared with the control (Fig. 6G). For the simultaneous dynamic control of pfkA and glmS, the two plasmids pBacm and pBacar were transformed into DN5-IM strain which dynamically inhibited pfkA, respectively. Strain DN5-IMM produced 8.63 g/L GlcNAc (Fig. 6H), indicating the effective regulation of GlcNAc production. The GlcNAc production of simultaneous down- and up-regulation of pfkA and glmS did not exhibit an obviously higher titer compared with that of pfkA or glmS single regulation. The intracellular FBP levels of strains DN5, DN5-IM, DN5-GAR, and DN5-IMM were also detected. This revealed that the FBP concentration in DN5-IM and DN5-IMM were lower than DN5, because when pfkA was dynamically repressed, more flux flowed into the GlcNAc production pathway in DN5-IM and DN5-IMM (Fig. 6I and K). Moreover, the FBP level in DN5-GAR did not change significantly compared with that in DN5, indicating that activated glmS led to more flux flowing into the GlcNAc production pathway without affecting the FBP level (Fig. 6J).

## 4. Discussion

Dynamic control has been employed in pathway engineering to rationally allocate intracellular resources for optimizing biosynthetic efficiency as the sensing signal changes, avoiding metabolic burden, waste, and toxic accumulation(Brockman and Prather, 2015; Gutteridge et al., 2007). In microbial fermentation, high glycolysis rates lead to overflow metabolism (Shimizu and Matsuoka, 2019), whereas low glycolysis rates lead to low growth efficiency. Therefore, understanding and controlling glycolysis flux is crucial for the improvement of biosynthesis efficiency.

Few studies have concerned the design and construction of biosensors that can sense metabolites in glycolysis, which is because central metabolites lack natural transcriptional regulators. Only two recent studies have reported the development of biosensors to respond metabolites in glycolysis; in one of the studies, an artificial transcription factor was created using computer-aided design to respond to D-erythrose 4-phosphate and glycerate-3-phosphate (Ding et al., 2020), and in the other, a pyruvate biosensor PdhR was explored to generate genetic circuits for reprograming the cellular central carbon metabolism of Bacillus subtilis (Xu et al., 2020).

In this study, a type of glycolysis flux biosensor was designed and created. This biosensor can sense glycolysis flux and dynamically regulate glycolysis pathway flux in a timely and precise manner. Because of the particularities of FBP, it can synchronize the upper and lower glycolysis flux through the feedforward activation of $\mathrm { \bf P y k , }$ , causing the linear relationship between the glycolysis flux and FBP pool. Such a flux-sensing biosensor allows the cells to recognize the ongoing glycolysis metabolism quantitatively(Litsios et al., 2018). Therefore, it can be used in the regulation of glycolysis for a series of biosynthetic pathways closely related to glycolysis, making the application more effective and extensive. Second, FBP is a key intermediate close to upper glycolysis, which can reflect the uptake and utilization of carbon sources; therefore, it is more effective to use FBP to control the key branch metabolic pathway of glycolysis, such as flux distribution at the G6P node, flux distribution toward amino sugar biosynthesis at the F6P node, and flux distribution toward aromatic compound biosynthesis at the PEP node.

The design principle of biosensors and their tuning are based on transcription regulation, which is determined by interactions between the molecular components (such as FBP, Cra, and its operator DNA) in equilibrium. Furthermore, their concentrations and interaction affinities determine the expression rate of regulated genes(Zong et al., 2017). Based on this, we tuned the biosensors in the following aspects: (1) the strength of the core promoters of Cra regulation, (2) the position of TFBS located on the promoter, (3) the affinity of Cra-box with the protein Cra (the sequence of Cra-box), (4) the expression level of Cra, and (5) the affinity of Cra with small-molecule FBP. These strategies transpired to be effective and suitable for tuning both activated and repressed glycolysis flux biosensors. By quantitatively described using the Hill equation, they offered guidance for unraveling the tuning mechanism of biosensors. Due to the global impact of the Cra regulator, we didn’t use those biosensors with overexpression of Cra or its mutants on plasmids for the practical application cases. In spite of this, the strategy of altering the ligand affinity of Cra by protein mutation is very effective and has guiding significance for function tuning of biosensors.

The essentiality of the tunability of biosensors was demonstrated in our dynamic control system. By employing series of finely calibrated glycolysis flux biosensors, the promoters P<sub>pam</sub> (from pL19) and P<sub>M23107</sub> (from pL09) on the control of pfkA and glmS exhibited the optimal effects for GlcNAc biosynthesis, indicating that they provided proper control of time and strength. Similarly, in the MVA dynamic control system, the repressing promoter Ppar (from pL25) exhibited its most efficient regulation in the EP-bifido strain BW-PR. Therefore, biosensors’ tunability is critical because it determines the on/off expression timing and strength of a target gene. Biosensors with varied dynamic ranges and thresholds, among other attributes, can provide custom-made regulation for every metabolic flux switch scene, as well as accomplish precise dynamic control and develop high production strains, especially for application in industrial settings.

Dual functional biosensors that up- and down-regulate more challenging metabolic pathways are necessary for more complicated and layered regulation in metabolic engineering. These dual regulators demonstrate both functionalities depending on the target TFBSs at specific promoters(De Paepe et al., 2017). In addition, our study demonstrated the position of TFBSs on the promoter as well as that structure change in TFs can alter the manner of regulation, which indicated the complexity and diversity of transcription regulation of bifunctional TFs. The detailed mechanism must be unraveled in the future. From an engineering point of view, these bifunctional modes of regulation bring numerous inspirational and luxuriant components to synthetic biology.

The successful application of our bifunctional glycolysis flux biosensor in metabolic engineering exhibited several advantages in the precise sensing of FBP and dynamic regulation of glycolysis flux for the biosynthesis of a variety of chemicals. Our strategy underlined the tunable principle of the biosensors that can reprogram metabolic flux in a precise and timely manner to maximize the yield in microbial cell factories.

figures.caption: Engineering workflow for positive-response construction and tuning. (A) The promoter architecture and characterization of the constructed positive-response biosensors pL01-pL10. (B) Tuning biosensors through the overexpression of Cra and modifying the metabolite-binding affinity of Cra. (C) Characterization of the constructed positive-response biosensors pL15, pL16, pL17, and pL18. The basis for the lines was Hill function fits. (D) The intracellular FBP concentration of strain harboring pL18 when different concentrations of FBP were added extracellularly. (CK-, no plasmid pL18; CK, 0 g/L acetate and 0 mM FBP; 0, 10 g/L acetate and 0 mM FBP; 0.001–400, 10 $_ { g / \mathrm { L } }$ acetate and 0.001–400 mM FBP). (E) The kinetic parameters of positive-response biosensors pL15, pL16, pL17 and pL18 including dynamic range and threshold $\mathrm { E C } _ { 5 0 } .$

Negative-response flux biosensor construction and tuning. (A) The promoters and characterization of the constructed negative-response biosensors pL19- pL30. The basis for the lines was Hill function fits. (B) The architecture of plasmid $\mathtt { p L 3 5 : }$ Cra with amino acid site mutation at 57, 58, 59, and 60 was cloned onto the plasmid with the promoter $\mathrm { P } _ { 2 3 1 0 2 }$ and the negative-response biosensor pL35 was characterized by dose-response curve. (C) The kinetic parameters of negative-response biosensors pL19, pL25 and pL35, including dynamic range and threshold $\mathrm { E C } _ { 5 0 } .$

Intracellular FBP and glycolysis flux detection in different deficiency strains with negative-response biosensor. (A) the relationship between intracellular FBP concentration and specific glucose consumption rate; (B) the relationship between intracellular FBP concentration and specific growth rate; (C) the relationship between intracellular FBP concentration and fluorescence value. The negative-response biosensor pL19 was used for detecting the glycolysis flux of these four strains. Fluorescence intensity was detected after the biosensor strains were cultured for 18 h.

Dynamic control of pfkA by the glycolysis flux biosensor in EP-bifido strains for high MVA production. (A) The engineered EP-bifido pathway and its dynamic control at the $p f k A$ target. (B) Genome manipulation at gene $p f k A$ promoter by integrating with negative-response biosensor-controlled promoters. (C) The relationship between cell growth and the MVA production of strain $\mathrm { B W } { \cdot } \mathrm { P } _ { z w f } { \therefore } \mathrm { P } _ { 2 3 1 0 9 } { \cdot }$ (D) The relationship between cell growth and the MVA production of strain BW-PR, and a comparison of the transcriptional level of pfkA in strains $\mathbf { B W } – \mathbf { P } _ { z w f } . : \mathbf { P } _ { 2 3 1 0 9 } \left( \mathbf { E } \right)$ ) and BW-PR (F). (G) A comparison of the in vivo FBP level in strains $\mathbf { B W - P } _ { z w f } { \boldsymbol { : : } } \mathbf { P } _ { 2 3 1 0 9 }$ and BW-PR. (H) The cell growth and MVA production of strain BW-PR in a 1-L fermenter.

Application of the flux biosensor in GlcNAc biosynthesis for improved production. (A) Dynamic control of GlcNAc production in E. coli by repressing pfkA and activating glmS. (B) Genome modification at pfkA gene promoter by integrating with negative-response biosensor-controlled promoters pL19 and pL25, and the construction of activation regulation in GlcNAc producing plasmid using positive-response biosensor promoters pL09 and pL18, respectively. (C–E) The cell growth of engineered E. coli strains DN5, DN5-PM, DN5-IM, DN5-GM, DN5-GAR, DN5-IMM, and DN5-IMAR. (F–H) The GlcNAc production of engineered E. coli strains DN5, DN5-PM, DN5-IM, DN5-GM, DN5-GAR, DN5-IMM, and DN5-IMAR.
